blocks.text: When an object is heated it starts to glow and gives out energy as radiation. This radiation depends only on the temperature of the object, not on its material or shape. As the temperature rises, its colour changes from dull red to bright yellow and then to white, showing that the radiation is shifting from longer wavelengths (infrared) towards shorter ones (ultraviolet). Real objects do not absorb or emit all radiation completely, so scientists consider an ideal object, the blackbody.

blocks.title: Blackbody
blocks.text: A blackbody is an object that absorbs all the radiation falling on it and also emits radiation at all wavelengths perfectly.

A good real example of a blackbody is a hollow cavity with a small hole and blackened inner walls, coated with soot (Fig 21.3). Radiation entering through the hole bounces around inside and is trapped. If the cavity is heated to a high enough temperature, the hole emits radiation of all wavelengths: blackbody radiation. Its pattern depends only on the temperature, and the energy given out increases as the temperature rises. A graph of intensity against wavelength (Fig 21.4) shows that the peak shifts to shorter wavelengths as the temperature rises: hotter blackbodies emit more energy at shorter wavelengths.

Stars such as the Sun behave like blackbody radiators. They generate their own energy by nuclear fusion, and it spreads into space as electromagnetic radiation covering a wide range of wavelengths in a continuous spectrum, similar to a blackbody spectrum. By studying the spectrum, scientists can estimate the star's surface temperature; each star has its own spectrum and so its own surface temperature.

blocks.title: Wien's displacement law
blocks.text: The wavelength lambda_max at which a blackbody emits radiation most intensely is inversely proportional to its surface temperature T: lambda_max is proportional to 1/T, or lambda_max T = b (21.3), where b is Wien's constant, 2.9 x 10^-3 m K.

As the temperature of a blackbody rises, its peak wavelength shifts to shorter values: hotter objects emit most strongly at shorter wavelengths (appearing blue or violet), cooler ones at longer wavelengths (appearing red or infrared). This shift explains the change in colour of heated objects and helps to determine the temperatures of stars.

blocks.title: Units of Wien's constant
blocks.text: The book writes b = 2.9 x 10^-3 'mK'; the unit is metre kelvin (m K), not millikelvin.

blocks.alt: Left: a ring-shaped cavity with a small gap (the hole); a blue ray enters and bounces around inside until absorbed. Right: graphs of intensity against wavelength from 0 to 3 micrometres for 5000, 4000, 3000 and 2000 K; each curve has a single peak, the 5000 K curve highest with its peak in the visible band, and a dashed purple line joins the peaks, which move to longer wavelengths as the temperature falls; lambda_max T = b = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K.
blocks.caption: Blackbody radiation (original diagram after Figs 21.3 and 21.4).
blocks.long_description: A hotter body gives out much more radiation at every wavelength, and its peak moves towards shorter, bluer wavelengths. Reading the peak wavelength of a star's spectrum gives its surface temperature.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: A blackbody is a perfect absorber and emitter of radiation. The cosmic microwave background radiation has an almost perfect blackbody spectrum, and even our bodies emit blackbody radiation in the infrared, which is why night-vision cameras can detect us in the dark. (The book also lists the microwave oven, but an oven's microwaves come from a magnetron at a single frequency, not from blackbody emission.)

The surface temperature of a star is 6000 K and the peak wavelength of its radiation is 480 nm. Another star has a peak wavelength of 320 nm. Calculate its surface temperature. Solution: lambda_max T = b, so lambda_max1 T1 = lambda_max2 T2 and T2 = lambda_max1 T1 / lambda_max2 = (480 x 10^-9 m x 6000 K)/(320 x 10^-9 m) = 9000 K.

blocks.prompt: Two objects are heated to different temperatures. One glows red-hot and the other white-hot. Which is hotter, and why?
blocks.explanation: The white-hot one: its emission peak has moved to shorter wavelengths, so it emits strongly across the whole visible range (white), while the red-hot one emits mainly at long (red) wavelengths.

blocks.prompt: If a star's peak wavelength is shorter, what does that tell us about its temperature?
blocks.explanation: It is hotter, since lambda_max T = constant.

items: Blackbody: absorbs all radiation and emits all wavelengths; cavity with a small hole.
Peak shifts to shorter wavelength as T rises.
Wien: lambda_max T = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K; stars behave as blackbodies.
